text: - **Documentum readiness — Jack O’Shea reset backfill expectations.** Backfill means writing properties to documents already stored in Documentum. PGD leadership had expected an imminent start, but more consistent model performance and clearer document-handling requirements are prerequisites. Jack reported that leadership understood both the progress and the remaining complexity after the preceding review. Model consistency remains an open readiness dependency; no separate remediation assignment or completion date was committed in this session. [00:03:11–00:05:01]

- **Repository controls — Jack O’Shea identified unresolved write-back rules.** The business requirements still need to establish whether low-confidence fields can enter Documentum, when model output should be withheld, and how duplicate documents should be handled. Permission to delete documents is also unresolved. These questions affect changes to existing repository records, not just extraction accuracy. The immediate process concern is defining what writing back actually entails, including the testing needed to support it. [00:04:13–00:04:37; 00:17:13–00:17:52]

- **Scope and accountability — Jack O’Shea acknowledged Apex Global-driven delivery friction.** The Q2 project vision had changed substantially through Q3 and Q4, with scope creep and insufficient product direction contributing to difficulty. Jack balanced that acknowledgment with satisfaction in the team’s work. Both attendees supported product-led executive communication, with engineers providing technical context rather than carrying commitments beyond their control. The intended change concerns who leads and owns the message, while preserving useful engineering participation. [00:05:18–00:05:56; 00:09:39–00:14:40]

- **Engineering focus — Amit Ayer clarified the team’s broader technical strengths.** Capabilities extend beyond data work to front-end development, software engineering, extraction, embeddings, and classification. Additional technical-lead capacity and stronger product oversight are intended to reduce competing coordination demands. Both attendees connected delivery problems to optimistic planning and changing direction, rather than a lack of technical ability. Clearer requirements and earlier escalation of dependencies were the practical improvements discussed for protecting engineering delivery. [00:06:10–00:09:33; 00:13:40–00:14:40]

- **Model economics — Amit Ayer flagged the cost of scaling DocIQ.** Amit recalled model-cost figures declining from nearly $1 to approximately $0.10; the measurement basis and document volume were unspecified. These remain approximate recollections rather than a verified per-document baseline or savings calculation. He also reported greater phase-two attention to sustainable human review, retraining, confidence governance, and image caching. That design attention connects extraction performance with operating cost, while implementation and measured benefits remain unverified. [00:14:56–00:15:37]

- **Work organization — Amit Ayer suggested separating remediation from enhancements.** His proposed Track A grouped staged backfill with DMT confidence alignment. A separate Track B grouped feature enhancements, including the file-upload interface and extraction-related work. This distinction would separate preparation for repository updates from additional functionality. The extraction detail was not developed further in the discussion. These were advisory work-track suggestions; no revised work breakdown, delivery assignment, or release commitment was adopted. [00:16:15–00:16:35]

- **Backfill validation — Amit Ayer suggested an optional 5,000-document pilot.** Rather than an all-or-nothing backfill, he described smaller pilot batches and offered 5,000 documents through the validation interface as one possibility. The proposed measurements were error calibration and throughput, giving leadership evidence about processing behavior while limiting operational exposure. The number was an example, not an agreed batch size. No pilot execution commitment, acceptance criteria, or measured results were established. [00:16:40–00:17:02]

- **Confidence routing — Amit Ayer suggested automatic handling above a proposed floor.** His advisory example used “Above 90” for automatic handling and lower-confidence results going to the validation interface for human triage, potentially through different queues. The number’s unit was unspecified, and behavior at exactly 90 was not defined. This remained a suggested routing concept rather than an approved threshold or implemented control; the business requirements for write-back remained open. [00:17:56–00:18:12]

- **Portfolio overlap — Jack O’Shea reported frustration with DocIQ-like initiatives.** Jack described parallel document-processing efforts elsewhere in the company as frustrating. DocIQ, LENS, and related charters provide the subjects for comparison, but the discussion supplied no named duplicate systems or quantified impact. Amit’s LENS experience concerned confidence metrics and additional data. The substantive question is how the initiatives fit together; consolidation, shared architecture, and changes to project charters remain open. [00:18:27–00:19:39]

- **File Upload — Reducing manual site-onboarding work.** The Q4 plan proposes a web upload location so users can submit documents without entering Documentum directly. This would automate intake currently handled by the DMT. The supporting waste analysis attributes approximately 25-plus hours of manual effort per site onboarding event to this opportunity; that figure is a planning justification, not a measured benefit already delivered by the proposed interface. File Upload effort is still TBD. Its value depends on connecting easier submission with reliable classification and repository routing, rather than simply adding another place to upload files. [S1; stmt-001, 00:00:00]

- **Technical Landscape — DocIQ classification, Documentum routing, and model feedback.** DocIQ is the Apex Global Analytics document-intelligence platform; its WIT Classifier determines the appropriate Documentum destination. The reviewed plan covers approximately 38–39 routing classifications. Subject-matter expert and DMT feedback feeds model improvement, with a separate workstream intended to automate the currently manual feedback and retraining loop. Planning estimates are one person for one sprint for classifier hardening and two people for two sprints for feedback automation. The drawings-classification goal is to move from 81% to 90% accuracy. These are planned capabilities and targets, rather than completed improvements. [S1; stmt-003, 00:05:34]

- **UI and Confidence Controls — Making automated changes visible and reviewable.** The proposed DocIQ interface would show classification confidence, extraction-field accuracy, processing costs, and error counts, giving the DMT a common view of repository maintenance and model performance. UI improvements carry an estimate of one person for one sprint. Confidence-threshold alignment is a separate, unestimated workstream: the DMT must agree the confidence level above which automated changes can proceed. The threshold therefore represents an operational approval boundary, not just a display setting. No numeric threshold was selected in the captured discussion. [S1; stmt-005, 00:07:28]

- **Historical Backfill — Quality checks constrain processing speed.** The approximately 650,000-document corpus requires staged processing. The reviewed plan calls for processing a small batch, assessing results, tuning, and repeating, with substantial hands-on work expected throughout the quarter. Identified Documentum samples have neither discipline nor document-type labels, making source quality a practical concern for classification and verification. The scheduling guidance discussed was sequencing rather than assuming a three-day bulk run. Batch sizes, processing dates, and detailed acceptance checks remain open; the corpus volume alone does not establish a completion schedule. [S1; stmt-008–stmt-010, 00:14:16–00:15:23]

- **ROT Hardening and Technology Extraction — Different capabilities with DMT involvement.** ROT—Redundant, Obsolete, Trivial—hardening would strengthen document-cleanup rules and automate their execution while allowing the DMT to review and approve recommended actions without developer involvement. Technology Extraction would add the ability to identify technology and equipment attributes within engineering documents, including testing and training with the DMT. Technology Extraction is estimated at one person for two sprints; ROT effort is TBD. These workstreams address different needs: repository hygiene and richer extracted information. Both depend on operational participation beyond model development alone. [S1; stmt-005–stmt-006, 00:07:28–00:08:34]

- **Scope Governance — Product, engineering, and operational responsibilities are distinct.** The discussion raised scope creep as an early risk, rather than reporting that expansion had already occurred. The stakeholder register identifies Jack O’Shea (Apex Global Analytics, Principal Product Manager) with requirements, roadmap, and milestone sign-offs; Scott Herold (Non-APEX AI Developer, Level 4 Lead / Contractor, NEE Analytics) with full-stack implementation, upload plumbing, UI, and automated ROT execution; and Eric Haskell (Apex Global Enterprises–PGD, PGD Technical Services Manager) as the operational sponsor and DMT leader. This separation matters because additional product requests and operational needs affect the same delivery capacity. [S2; stmt-006, 00:08:34]

- **Staffing Continuity — Support and replacement coverage remain alternatives.** The staffing discussion considered strengthening existing delivery capability alongside possible personnel replacement coverage. This is separate from processing the historical document backfill. The concrete follow-ups are to check an existing workstream assignment, conduct a delivery check-in, and obtain further input on staffing. The supporting stakeholder register describes enablement as a settled direction, while the captured dialogue ends with further consultation. The recap therefore retains an open staffing choice. Neither a replacement assignment nor an overlap period was established in the session. [stmt-011–stmt-017, 00:16:50–00:21:38; S2]

- **Related Document-Intelligence Work — Potential overlap warrants a follow-up conversation.** The closing discussion identified possible overlap between DocIQ and other document-intelligence engagements or charters. The overlap was described at the level of similar use cases; specific shared components, dependencies, or duplicate deliverables were not identified. Amit Ayer accepted a follow-up conversation on that topic. Separately, the Q4 plan still has unestimated work for File Upload, confidence alignment, backfill management, and ROT hardening. The overlap discussion adds a coordination question, not an approved consolidation of work or a revised Q4 delivery commitment. [S1; stmt-020–stmt-021, 00:23:12–00:23:25]

- **Traci framed Q4 as architecture-first while keeping charter approval tied to measurable outcomes.** Traci explained that Jarvis is a new application requiring architecture and infrastructure before larger workflow outcomes can be delivered. She used the analogy that the foundation must be established “before we can build the house.” The charter therefore needs to explain why Q4 may carry a smaller measurable return while still presenting enough quantified value to support approval. [00:00:33–00:01:35]

- **Amit challenged the initial scope and refused to make PartnerAdvisory responsible for inventing client value assumptions.** Amit said, “I don’t want to be on the hook to develop value drivers from scratch,” and pressed Traci to clarify the request. Traci responded that she wanted general guidance on ways to measure AI-enabled workflow value—not help writing the charter or performing the client’s calculations. Amit acknowledged the clarification after describing himself as “crossed up” by the original framing. [00:01:36–00:03:08; 00:05:20–00:07:39]

- **Traci confirmed the current $1.3 million figure is based on labor time savings and still depends on a developing spreadsheet.** Traci said the figure reflects saved time and follows a method used in other approved charters. She lacked access to the working spreadsheet during this debrief because it was still being built, creating a temporary review constraint. The meeting accepted the figure as the current baseline for discussion, not as a newly validated or approved financial result. [00:04:15–00:05:14; 00:05:42–00:07:18; 00:09:24–00:10:02]

- **Amit proposed cycle-time compression as one possible measure beyond raw labor hours.** Amit distinguished small pockets of saved employee time—what he called “ghost savings”—from a measurable reduction in calendar turnaround. He suggested examining whether Jarvis could shorten design-review milestones and thereby improve asset utilization or cash flow. He explicitly characterized this as brainstorming rather than industry best practice. Examples such as reducing 21 days to three or four days were illustrative, not forecasts. [00:07:45–00:11:09]

- **Amit proposed defect reduction and rework avoidance as a second possible value driver.** Amit explained that design discrepancies become more expensive when discovered later, particularly after reaching field construction. He suggested evaluating whether Jarvis could cross-reference drawings against engineering criteria and catch issues earlier. The example of identifying three to five defects per quarter illustrated the measurement concept; it was not a validated target. Traci confirmed that this value was outside the current $1.3 million labor-savings baseline. [00:11:14–00:12:45]

- **Traci mapped the proposed drivers to the Jarvis design-review workflow.** Traci identified design review and retrieval as the strongest application for faster turnaround, citing an example of reducing review time from 12 hours to one hour. She separated reduced search clicks from reduced review effort and explained that Jarvis may also eliminate repeat meetings among five reviewers. For rework avoidance, she emphasized better drawing-review accuracy, fewer repeated reviews, and the possibility of catching discrepancies that a human reviewer might miss. [00:17:22–00:20:50]

- **Amit and Traci created a working measurement structure while leaving monetization to the client.** They organized the discussion into four fields: value category, Jarvis application, metric, and monetization. Candidate metrics included design-review turnaround time and the number of field design discrepancies avoided per quarter. Amit stressed that APEX must agree to each driver and assign its dollar value; PartnerAdvisory can identify the drivers, provide useful metrics, and review the resulting calculations. [00:13:47–00:16:53; 00:20:56–00:21:47]

- **Amit and Traci narrowed the usable value story and identified a double-counting risk.** Amit excluded capacity scaling and workforce-reduction claims because those topics exceeded the intended charter discussion. Traci agreed that the immediate objective was to provide enough support to advance the draft. They identified cycle-time compression as potentially overlapping with the existing $1.3 million baseline, while rework avoidance appeared potentially net new. Amit also committed to attend the 04:00 PM ET follow-up meeting. [00:22:03–00:23:42]

- **Sharon Diaram outlined permit-compliance extraction as a practical Jarvis workflow.** An uploaded permit would be analyzed to separate boilerplate language from conditions requiring action, such as submitting a report to an agency within 120 days. The initial output would be a PDF recorded in project memory. Sharon described automated task creation and compliance-team notification as a possible later version, tentatively mentioning a future quarter rather than setting an approved release date. [00:00:33–00:01:20]

- **Sharon Diaram and Amit Ayer established Power BI as the practical source for the WBS auditor.** The proposed auditor would examine prior-month or prior-quarter actuals, identify new or anomalous charges, identify the charging party, and draft an inquiry email. Amit asked whether the first phase would connect directly to SAP or use existing reporting. Sharon selected Power BI, explaining that the team already receives a large spreadsheet that feeds Power BI, avoiding the initial burden of securing direct IT access to specialized reports. [00:01:24–00:02:32]

- **Sharon Diaram cataloged meeting-memory and spatial-file workflows alongside the main candidates.** The meeting-scribe concept would extract decisions and insights from transcripts or summaries and record them in project memory. A later concept could translate spoken commitments into project-management updates. Sharon also described routing spatial files into a web map, addressing the recurring need to send Jira requests to the GIS team for uploads. These ideas remained part of the broader workflow catalog rather than the selected initial business-case focus. [00:02:42–00:03:41]

- **Daniel Brankin and Taylor Mercer identified design review as the preferred initial quick-win candidate.** Sharon characterized the workflows as relatively straightforward once a common upload-and-trigger framework exists because the early pattern is read-only: ingest a document, run a specialized agent, and return a PDF result. Daniel favored the workflow with the greatest time and financial impact, and Traci recorded design review as the preference. The Q1 reference clarified the intended planning horizon but did not establish a delivery deadline or implementation authorization. [00:06:34–00:08:24]

- **Amit Ayer explained that orchestration can evolve in parallel with the workflows.** He described an orchestrator as a reasoning or routing layer that selects the appropriate agent, coordinates communication among agents, and can use deterministic rules, machine learning, or an LLM. The workflows can begin independently; orchestration becomes more useful as overlap and routing logic emerge. Amit recommended developing it alongside increasingly defined workflows so the team can test whether each trigger reaches the correct path, while keeping it optional rather than making it an upfront dependency. [00:03:59–00:04:35; 00:09:52–00:11:22]

- **Sharon Diaram connected the business case to fragmented project-management practices across APEX development.** She described information and decisions being tracked in Excel, OneNote, or the memory of experienced employees, creating repeated effort when project history must be rebuilt or transferred. The working model covered approximately 60 development employees and several potential sources of time savings. Sharon viewed design review as the most significant opportunity, while acknowledging that agent-creation infrastructure itself carries limited direct savings and mainly supports future workflows. [00:05:06–00:06:40]

- **Amit Ayer challenged the 540-hours-per-month assumption and broadened the ROI discussion.** He asked whether transmission and solar developers would complete comparable reviews at the assumed frequency and warned that the result could be challenged as “soft savings” if every utilization assumption had to hold simultaneously. He suggested considering reduced external engineering-consultant spend and avoided downstream construction impacts as supporting evidence. Sharon agreed that the concern was valid and connected it to consultant spend, while noting the difficulty of obtaining enough data to quantify the effect. [00:11:49–00:13:47]

She also committed to follow up on the identities of the technical resources and the Forge locations available to support the work. A separate question remains open about whether NEA already has a related construction-drawing initiative that could overlap with the preferred design-review workflow. [00:14:23–00:16:34]

- **Sharon Diaram kept the project-management layer tool-neutral and called for reuse of existing enterprise capabilities.** Sharon described a Q4 dashboard and GIS view that presents projects and draws data from SAP, then compared the needed workflow capability with Navigator, Microsoft Project, monday.com, and other available tools. She asked that the Charter remove the explicit monday.com reference so the team could evaluate alternatives. The broader question is whether Navigator, Forge, or capabilities elsewhere in APEX already provide components that Jarvis can reuse instead of rebuilding them. [00:01:05–00:05:00]

- **Sharon Diaram defined living project memory as a core Jarvis foundation.** She said Jarvis must retain more than information from LAMS and SAP. Its project context should also include tasks, meeting minutes, decisions, changing schedules, and eventually relevant email activity. Each interaction should make the project record more useful for later questions. This would allow an agent to explain what changed, summarize prior decisions, and surface outstanding work without requiring users to reconstruct project history across dashboards, spreadsheets, notes, and disconnected communications. [00:06:00–00:07:00]

- **Sharon Diaram mapped a proposed flow from Jarvis chat to LAMS, dashboards, and enterprise documents.** Her example allowed a user to request a date change through the Jarvis interface, have the revised value appear in the dashboard, and find the same value in the LAMS project record. She viewed LAMS and new project-management tables as more practical initial write destinations than SAP or GIS. She also proposed retrieving the latest design from Documentum and a source referred to as WAMS, with future saving or writeback subject to system access and governance. [00:08:15–00:12:00]

- **Sharon Diaram made transcript-to-task processing central to the proposed project workflow.** She described uploading a meeting transcript into Jarvis so the system could identify the relevant project, apply its stored context, extract decisions and tasks, and route work to the appropriate subject-matter expert. She called the full project-management workflow “fundamental to what Jarvis is” because it could reduce manual meeting recaps, Excel and OneNote updates, and repeated requests for status. The architecture must therefore connect project memory, task creation, specialist agents, and the user’s outstanding-work view. [00:39:00–00:41:15]

- **Amit Ayer required a staged approval step before any agent changes enterprise data.** Amit described a control in which Jarvis drafts a LAMS date change or document upload, shows the proposed difference, and waits for approval before applying it. He later summarized the principle plainly: an agent cannot silently modify a live database, and unrestricted autonomy does not work in an enterprise setting. This control becomes especially important when connecting Jarvis to LAMS, SAP, GIS, Outlook, Documentum, or other governed systems. [00:14:15–00:16:45; 00:36:15–00:38:00]

- **Amit Ayer recommended using Q1 to strengthen the Jarvis platform before broader writeback.** He supported concentrating near-term effort on the platform, project memory, agent framework, and workflows that avoid direct changes to existing enterprise systems. Writeback would follow only after architecture, data governance, system authorization, and organizational comfort are addressed. References to Q2, Q3, and later periods were planning scenarios rather than fixed delivery dates. The working sequence therefore favors useful read, retrieval, drafting, and human-review capabilities while the more sensitive integration path is evaluated. [00:15:45–00:17:30; 00:34:00–00:37:30]

- **Daniel Brankin and Amit Ayer defined “zero manual data entry” as the intended Jarvis user experience.** Daniel described opening Jarvis in the morning, reviewing outstanding tasks, and approving or rejecting recommendations while agents perform the supporting work. Amit agreed that building another scheduler requiring engineers to type tasks and dates would merely reproduce Navigator or Excel and waste time. This established a clear product test: project-management features should reduce administrative entry, not shift it into a new interface. Humans should review consequential recommendations while Jarvis assembles context, prepares work, and tracks follow-through. [00:33:00–00:35:15; 00:45:15–00:46:45]

- **Daniel Brankin proposed documenting seven simple workflow candidates that avoid direct enterprise writeback.** The candidates were framed as proofs of concept rather than seven production commitments. An email-review workflow was one example, but it depends on whether NEA permits Jarvis to connect to Outlook. The group distinguished drafting or reviewing email from allowing an agent to send messages or update enterprise records. Outlook access is therefore an open dependency, while project memory and other foundation work may proceed with fewer write permissions and prepare Jarvis for later capabilities. [00:20:45–00:22:00; 00:42:00–00:43:45]

- **Daniel Brankin and Amit Ayer identified design review and document retrieval as the clearest measurable time savers.** Daniel said the organization conducts roughly two to five design reviews per month, each taking about four hours, and presented planning figures including nine hours saved per person per month and a 540-hour estimate. Amit characterized design review as the strongest example of true automation because AI would inspect complex drawings against criteria. He ranked document retrieval and living memory next, citing approximately 12 clicks to find a file and about 20 minutes spent searching SharePoint. All benefit figures require bottom-up validation. [00:22:30–00:26:15; 00:31:45–00:32:30]

- **Taylor Mercer, Amit Ayer, and Daniel Brankin tested whether expansion from 10 to 60 users belongs in the Q1 benefit story.** Traci asked whether wider adoption of the Q4 capability should add measurable savings. Amit argued that expanding a tested baseline could yield immediate benefits even before new code is added. Daniel initially challenged whether those savings could be attributed to Q1 work, then accepted the distinction after further discussion. The Charter therefore needs to separate benefits from broader adoption from benefits created by new Q1 functionality, while retaining the $90 hourly rate and other inputs as estimates. [00:26:15–00:31:15]

- **Taylor Mercer and Amit Ayer established the immediate Charter coordination path while resource assumptions stayed tentative.** The team discussed two developers as the expected allocation, with 10/01/2026 described tentatively and 10/05/2026 characterized as more likely. Daniel emphasized that Reid Schenk (Apex Global Analytics, Executive Director) wanted a clear statement of expected Q1 value. Traci agreed to update the Charter after receiving the finalized source material and moved a follow-up review to 4:00 PM ET, subject to room acceptance. Amit planned to review the final choices before editing the document. [00:18:00–00:19:30; 00:44:00–00:45:00; 00:47:00–00:49:30]
